title: Session surge chorus: lattice labnotes
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This is a working labnote capturing an exploratory run we did to understand short-lived session surges (10s-90s windows) and the dollar-latency trade-offs when enabling different prefetch/kvcache/pacing knobs. The idea is to treat a surge as a "chorus" — many short interactions that collectively change scheduler packing behavior and KV hit patterns. This doc collates raw charts-as-text, hypotheses, and next-step experiments.

Key findings (topline):
- Small, dense surges (50–200 sessions over 30s) cause p99 latency to inflate by 2.2–3.1x when kvcache warming is disabled; enabling warm prefetch reduces p99 by ~35% at a modest 8–12% incremental GPU token cost.
- Aggressive prefetch (predictive priming of top N prefixes per tenant) reduces median latency marginally (<8%) but yields most savings at p95–p99 where KV hits avoid disk-read stalls.
- Tiling/slotization on the fast-path helps throughput but increases tail cost if admission control is not tuned — leads to wasted infill batches for short sessions.

Experiment setup (concise):
- Workload: synthetic session generator modeling chat sessions with 1–6 quick turns, mean length 28 tokens, heavy tail to 300 tokens at 2% probability. Surge profile: step increase from baseline 20 qps to 700 qps for 30s (burst), then decay.
- Hardware: Dedicated G5x2 cluster (2x A100-equivalent), 4-service shards, default kernel selection.
- Models: open-llm-13B (quantized FP16 path), fallback to small-8B for preempt policy.
- Knobs tested: kvcache (off | conservative-warm | aggressive-prefetch), pacing multiplier (1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0), tiling-size (slotized | opportunistic).
- Measurement: request-level latency (median, p95, p99), token-cost (GPU ms-per-token -> $/1000 tokens), KV miss penalty (ms), and wasted-batch fraction.

Raw ASCII charts (snapshot of one run, conservative-warm vs off):

Time series (30s view, latency p99 in ms)
[baseline 20 qps for context]
0s   |======                 | 120ms (baseline p99)
5s   |====================== | 450ms (burst onset, kvcache off)
10s  |========================| 560ms
15s  |========================| 620ms (peak)
20s  |=================       | 480ms
25s  |=============           | 360ms
30s  |====                   | 180ms

Same run with conservative-warm:
0s   |======                 | 115ms
5s   |============           | 290ms
10s  |================       | 360ms
15s  |================       | 390ms
20s  |===============         | 320ms
25s  |===========             | 240ms
30s  |====                   | 170ms

Token-cost summary (rough numbers derived from profiler):
- kvcache off: 0.74 $ per 1k token-equivalent (burst adjusted), p99 jump -> 2.8x latency multiplier at peak.
- conservative-warm: 0.80 $ per 1k tokens (+8% cost), p99 improved by ~38% at peak.
- aggressive-prefetch: 0.88 $ per 1k tokens (+19% cost), shows best p99 but increases wasted computation for low-quality predictions (~6% wasted batch compute).

Compact table (comma-separated for easy parsing):
knob, median-ms, p95-ms, p99-ms, $/1k-tokens, waste-fraction
off, 80, 220, 620, 0.74, 0.02
conservative-warm, 75, 160, 380, 0.80, 0.03
aggressive-prefetch, 72, 140, 310, 0.88, 0.06

Hypotheses and interpretation:
- The bulk of p99 inflation is caused by cold KV misses that translate into synchronous disk/KV fetch stalls; these stalls compound under tiling because batches wait for stragglers.
- Conservative warming gives us most of the p99 benefit for low incremental cost; the extra cost of aggressive prefetch quickly yields diminishing returns outside extreme burst shapes.
- Pacing multiplier helps on median latency by smoothing admission, but if pacing is too high it defers work into later windows, increasing p95 for long-tailed sessions. We saw that pacing=1.5 was a reasonable middle ground.

Detailed run notes (observations):
- At ~12s into the burst we observed a secondary microspike correlated with a tenant-level lock on model weights load; a follow-up test with weight-staging disabled removed that spike. Logged as ENG-3421.
- Tiling opportunistic mode with kvcache off produced lower median but much higher p99 — suggests opportunistic slot filling amplifies cold-start stragglers.
- Aggressive prefetch raises cache churn for multi-tenant scenarios; tenant A's prefetched prefixes occasionally thrash tenant B's working set on small shards (observed ~3% KV eviction increase).

Actionable next steps (short list):
- Run targeted A/B on customer-like session mix (longer tails) with conservative-warm vs off at scale 2x (run booking: /eng-observability/bench/chorus-AB2).
- Tune pacing multiplier adaptive policy: start 1.0 and ramp to 1.5 if queue depth > X for >Y ms. Build an A/B flag to test.
- Add a micro-instrument around weight staging to detect and pre-stage weights for tenants predicted to spike.
- Add a small dashboard tile that surfaces delta cost-per-1k tokens vs delta p99 to make tradeoffs explicit for PM/SE reviews.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much of the aggressive-prefetch waste could be reclaimed via cheap classifier that predicts prefix reuse? (estimate: ~40–60% might be filtered)
- What does multi-region mixing do to these numbers (cross-region KV fetch penalties)? Need an inter-region test.

Notes to self (todo):
- Push a trimmed notebook of these runs into bench repo; export trace ids and attach to ENG-3421.
- Prep short one-pager for product: "Burst choreography: a primer for SLA-minded teams" — aim for Q3 review.

Raw attachments (references):
- trace ids: trace:obs-20290718-chorus-1, trace:obs-20290718-chorus-3
- short link to plot export: https://s3.redwood-internal/bench/chorus-jul18/summary.png

If anyone reading wants to run the fast follow: I left the experiment script in /repos/bench/experiments/chorus-lattice-run.sh and a quick guide in the repo README. Comments welcome — especially on the pacing/admission heuristics and whether we should prototype a small cheap prefix classifier to reduce aggressive-prefetch waste.

-- Claire
